papers.title: Elevated erythrocyte membrane pS42-α-synuclein in Parkinson's disease and its changes following plasma cross-incubation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Blood biomarkers for pathological α-synuclein in Parkinson's disease (PD) are confounded by hemolysis and hemoglobin. Erythrocyte membrane-bound α-synuclein may overcome these challenges. OBJECTIVE: To investigate whether erythrocyte membrane-bound α-synuclein is altered in PD and whether it changes following plasma cross-incubation. METHODS: Erythrocyte membranes from patients with PD and healthy controls were isolated and analyzed by phosphoproteomics to identify phosphorylation sites. Digital western blotting was used for targeted quantification of α-synuclein species. Plasma cross-incubation was performed in a subset of participants. RESULTS: Phosphorylation patterns of erythrocyte membrane-associated α-synuclein differed between PD and controls. Several phosphorylation sites were detected. Among them, serine 42 (pS42-α-syn) showed the strongest signal and was selected for further analysis. pS42-α-syn levels were higher in PD than in controls (median 0.055 vs. 0.007, P < 0.0001). After plasma cross-incubation, pS42-α-syn levels decreased in both groups. The median percentage reduction was numerically greater in PD than in controls (49.88% vs. 27.44%), although the between-group difference did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.052). Changes in total α-synuclein did not reach statistical significance after plasma cross-incubation (P = 0.23 in controls and P = 0.08 in PD patients). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis showed good discriminative performance. CONCLUSIONS: Erythrocyte membrane pS42-α-syn is increased in PD. These findings support erythrocyte membrane pS42-α-syn as a peripheral phospho-α-synuclein signal associated with PD.

papers.title: Recent advances in the management of Lewy body dementia: evaluating progress and future directions.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Lewy body dementia (LBD), encompassing dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD), is progressive and heterogeneous in clinical presentation and underlying pathobiology. LBD substantially impacts patient function, independence, and quality of life. Current therapies are symptomatic, and disease-modifying therapies are not established. Advances in in vivo AREAS COVERED: This review examines the complex spectrum of LBD, including DLB, PDD, and prodromal states of MCI-LB and PD-MCI. Advances in biomarkers and biological frameworks are considered along with limitations in DLB. Recent pharmacological and non-pharmacological clinical trials are highlighted. The authors offer commentary on the challenges and opportunities for current and future research and care in LBD. EXPERT OPINION: LBD remains a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge. papers.title: ProSAAS overexpression arrests progression of motor deficits in a rat alpha-synuclein model of Parkinson's disease.
β-Cyclodextrin-Complexed 1,8-Cineole Attenuates Motor Deficits and Preserves Tyrosine Hydroxylase Immunoreactivity in a Reserpine-Induced Mouse Model of Parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic dysfunction and motor impairment. Natural compounds have emerged as promising candidates for neuroprotection and symptomatic relief in experimental models of PD. This study investigated the effects of β-cyclodextrin-complexed 1,8-cineole (CIN) in a reserpine (RES)-induced mouse model of parkinsonism. Male mice were treated with RES (0.1 mg/kg, s.c., every 48 h) and/or CIN (5 mg/kg, p.o., once daily) for 30 days. Behavioral assessments evaluated motor, sensorimotor, and locomotor function. Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and α-synuclein immunoreactivity were assessed by immunohistochemistry. Repeated RES administration induced progressive motor and sensorimotor impairments and reduced TH immunoreactivity in mesencephalic dopaminergic nuclei. CIN treatment significantly reduced catalepsy, vacuous chewing movements, and chin tremors and improved sensorimotor performance in the adhesive removal test. These behavioral effects were accompanied by preservation of TH immunoreactivity in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA). However, CIN did not significantly alter hippocampal α-synuclein immunoreactivity. These findings indicate that β-cyclodextrin-complexed CIN attenuates motor and sensorimotor deficits and is associated with preservation of dopaminergic markers in a RES-induced mouse model of parkinsonism. These results support further investigation of CIN as a neuroactive compound in experimental models of PD.

papers.title: Neurodegenerative diseases in Sub-Saharan Africa: diagnostic invisibility, biological heterogeneity and a precision-neuroscience agenda.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are increasingly recognised in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), but the principal scientific challenge is no longer simply to document a presumed hidden burden. It is to determine how much of the observed heterogeneity reflects underlying neurobiology and how much arises from age structure, case ascertainment, culturally sensitive phenotyping and unequal access to neurological diagnosis. This critical narrative review synthesises evidence from 2000 to July 2026 across epidemiology, disease mechanisms, genomics, biomarkers, environmental exposures, therapeutics and health systems, using Tanzania as an illustrative case rather than a regional proxy. Community studies demonstrate substantial diagnostic invisibility, while recent African-ancestry research shows that inclusion of genetically diverse populations can reveal mechanisms that are poorly captured in ancestry-restricted datasets. The glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) rs3115534-G Parkinson's disease signal provides a proof of principle, linking an African-ancestry-enriched association to altered ribonucleic acid (RNA) splicing and glucocerebrosidase biology. Emerging plasma biomarkers and ancestry-aware genomics create a route from syndromic diagnosis towards biological characterisation, but thresholds and models require population-specific validation. This review proposes that the next phase of African neurodegeneration research should integrate culturally valid phenotype, biomarkers, imaging, genomics, measured exposures and longitudinal outcomes from inception. Such platforms could distinguish measurement artefact from biological variation, improve regional diagnosis and test the global generalisability of prevailing models of neurodegeneration.

papers.title: The mechanism of the parkin-CMA-NLRP3-PANoptosis signaling axis in Parkinson's disease: From molecular basis to therapeutic strategies.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder. Existing clinical interventions merely relieve symptoms and cannot reverse progressive neuronal injury. Neuroinflammation and dysregulated programmed cell death are central pathological drivers of PD. PANoptosis is an integrated pan-programmed cell death, can simultaneously trigger apoptosis, pyroptosis and necroptosis, with the NOD‑like receptor family pyrin domain‑containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome serving as a core molecular hub for PANoptosis initiation. Apart from its well‑characterized role in mitophagy, Parkin directly interacts with NLRP3 and mediates K63‑linked ubiquitination at the NLRP3‑K353 residue. This post‑translational modification targets NLRP3 for degradation through chaperone‑mediated autophagy (CMA), which suppresses excessive PANoptosis and preserves dopaminergic neuron survival. This review systematically delineates the molecular framework of the Parkin‑CMA‑NLRP3‑PANoptosis signaling axis. We further discuss its functional crosstalk with canonical PD‑associated pathological events, including α‑synuclein (α‑syn) aggregation and mitochondrial dysfunction, and summarize translational progress of small‑molecule compounds and gene therapies targeting individual components within this cascade. Critical bottlenecks are also addressed, such as unresolved molecular regulatory details, limitations of preclinical animal models, poor blood‑brain barrier permeability of candidate agents, and obstacles for early therapeutic intervention. This work intends to uncover promising targets for PD disease‑modifying treatments and support the advancement of precision therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Angiotensin II-induced hypertension does not exacerbate α-SYNUCLEIN pathology in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by progressive degeneration of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons accompanied by chronic neuroinflammation and α-SYNUCLEIN (α-SYN) aggregation. Increasing evidence suggests that cardiovascular comorbidities, including arterial hypertension, may contribute to neurodegenerative processes through vascular dysfunction and sustained inflammatory signaling. However, whether hypertension directly exacerbates α-SYN-induced neurodegeneration and inflammasome activation remains unclear. papers.title: Gene-based association analysis of depression risk among European ancestry Parkinson's disease patients.
papers.abstract: Depression is one of the most common and disabling non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its genetic basis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the genetic contributions to depression in PD by estimating the burden from common as well as low-frequency single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within genes previously implicated in PD or depression risk among European ancestry PD patients from three population-based studies. Using gene-based association analyses (SKAT, Burden, and SKAT-O) in the PASIDA, PEG, and PPMI studies, we evaluated SNP sets in gene regions previously linked to PD or depression. Among PD-related genes, meta-analysis identified a significant association between KRTCAP2 and self-reported depression diagnosis in PD (SKAT-O p = 4.33 × 10⁻⁵), which remained significant after false discovery rate correction. A higher genetic burden in KRTCAP2 was associated with 20% increased odds of depression (OR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.04-1.38). TRAF5 and LRRK2 showed marginal associations. Among depression-related genes, SPPL3 and ERBB4 were associated with depression diagnosis history, and FNIP2 was associated with current depressive symptoms. The PD polygenic risk score was not associated with depression in PD, while a higher depression polygenic risk score was significantly associated with increased odds of depression diagnosis in both cohorts and the meta-analysis (OR = 1.26, 95% CI: 1.13-1.40). Our findings highlight immune-related genes such as KRTCAP2 and TRAF5 as potential contributors to depression in PD. Additionally, the depression PRS shows statistically significant association with depression diagnosis in PD, suggesting that a general depression-related genetic liability contributes to this non-motor feature in PD. papers.title: The FOG-COA Protocol: Validation of Freezing of Gait Clinical Outcomes Assessments in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: The development and evaluation of novel treatment options for freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease have been limited by an ambiguous definition and lack of standardized clinical outcome assessments (COAs) that 1) reliably assess FOG severity, 2) are responsive to change, and 3) capture patient-relevant impact. To address these gaps, working groups from the International Consortium on FOG (ICFOG) developed a clinician-rated outcome-the Giladi Protocol for assessing FOG severity (GP-FOG), and a patient-reported outcome-the FOG Quality of Life questionnaire (FOG-QOL). The FOG-COA project will evaluate the conceptual framework and psychometric properties of these COAs to determine their fit-for-purpose in clinical trials. A total of 105 freezers and 35 non-freezers from seven international centers will complete the GP-FOG in the dopaminergic OFF and ON states during two separate visits (7-14 days apart). FOG annotations from video recordings will be used to assess criterion validity. OFF and ON GP-FOG scores from two trained raters at Visit 1, as well as within-rater scores across visits, will examine reliability. Responsiveness will be evaluated by comparing effect sizes between OFF and ON GP-FOG scores. Patient meaningfulness will be assessed through the association between patient-perceived FOG severity and GP-FOG scores. Participants will complete the FOG-QOL at each visit to assess test-retest reliability and validity against the NFOGQ and PDQ-8. A subset of freezers will undergo cognitive interviews to identify relevant daily life FOG impacts and evaluate FOG-QOL meaningfulness. Collectively, this work will advance standardized, sensitive, and meaningful FOG-COAs, supporting regulatory-grade endpoints and the development of a multi-dimensional outcome framework.

papers.title: [Burden on the caregiver of people with disabilities secondary to neurological damage. A multicenter study in Argentina].
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Caregiver burden encompasses the physical, financial, and psychosocial impact of caring for a person, constituting a risk factor for the deterioration of the caregiver's health and quality of life. The primary objective was to quantify caregiver burden in primary caregivers of individuals with disabilities secondary to neurological damage in four healthcare centers in Argentina. The secondary objective was to explore its association with the duration of disability, level of functional independence, hours of care, and the caregiver's gender. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a multicenter, prospective, cross-sectional, observational study conducted between March and September 2025. Caregivers with at least three months of continuous caregiving were included. Sociodemographic and clinical data were collected from both the caregiver and the patient. Caregiver burden was assessed using the Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI). Multiple regression models were applied to identify predictors of the ZBI score. RESULTS: 116 caregivers participated (77% women, mean age 54 years). Seventy-two percent of patients presented with caregiver burden (50% severe; 22% mild). The patients were mostly men with stroke, Parkinson's disease, or traumatic brain injury, with a mean duration of two years. None of the independent variables showed a statistically significant association with the ZBI score. CONCLUSION: A high prevalence of caregiver burden was detected, without identifying statistically significant predictors, highlighting the impact of caring for a family member with a disability. The predominance of female caregivers underscores the central role of women in caregiving. These findings highlight the need to integrate caregiver-focused interventions into neuro-rehabilitation programs.

papers.title: Habitual Diet, Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis, and α-Synucleinopathy Conversion in Isolated Rapid Eye Movement (REM) Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accumulating evidence indicates that habitual diet, including plant-based dietary patterns, is associated with neurodegenerative α-synucleinopathy risk. However, the role of diet and its correlation with the gut microbiome in prodromal α-synucleinopathy, specifically among patients with isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate dietary patterns, their interplay with gut microbial dysbiosis, and longitudinal effects on neurodegenerative progression in iRBD patients. METHODS: We recruited 287 iRBD patients and 208 age- and sex-matched controls. Plant-based diet indices (PDIs) were derived from food frequency questionnaires. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed in 456 subjects for diet-microbiome analyses. After a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 45 (15.7%) iRBD patients converted to α-synucleinopathies. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the associations between diet and neurodegenerative outcomes. RESULTS: We found that iRBD patients exhibited lower healthful PDIs (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.48 [0.29-0.80], P = 0.005) but higher consumption of unhealthful plant-based foods (refined grains, sweets, and sweeteners). Diet-microbiome interaction analysis identified dietary associations for 84.3% of iRBD-related gut microbes, including co-occurrence between healthful PDI and Clostridium sp. AF20-17LB. Longitudinally, four dietary factors and five iRBD-related microbes were associated with neurodegenerative outcomes; specifically, higher coffee consumption was linked to a lower risk of progression to α-synucleinopathy (aHR [95% CI]: 0.30 [0.11-0.78], P = 0.01). Furthermore, mediation analyses indicated that the iRBD-enriched species Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans mediated the association between unhealthful PDI and dementia-first conversion. papers.title: zDHHC11 is a Common Palmitoyltransferase Regulating Microglia-Mediated Neuroinflammation across Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation is a shared feature across Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and diabetic cognitive impairment (DCI), but the convergent molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated whether protein S-palmitoylation serves as a common regulator of microglial neuroinflammation across distinct neurodegenerative diseases etiologies and aimed to identify the key palmitoyltransferase involved. METHODS: In vivo ND models (APP/PS1 for AD, MPTP for PD, STZ/high-fat diet for DCI) and in vitro BV2 microglial models stimulated with amyloid-β (Aβ), lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or high glucose (HG) were established. Microglial morphology, inflammatory responses, and the TLR4/MyD88 pathway were assessed by immunofluorescence, RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and ELISA. Protein palmitoylation levels were evaluated using 2-BP and ABE assays. Palmitoyltransferase expression profiling was performed, and protein-level validation was conducted both in vitro and in vivo. Subsequently, the identified common enzyme, zDHHC11, was knocked down by siRNA to determine its functional role. RESULTS: All three ND models showed robust microglial activation with a pro-inflammatory amoeboid morphology. Aβ, LPS, and HG each upregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines and activated the TLR4/MyD88 pathway in BV2 cells. Palmitoylation inhibition with 2-BP attenuated cytokine production, and all three stimuli increased total protein palmitoylation. Among all palmitoyltransferases screened, zDHHC11 was uniquely and consistently upregulated by all three stimuli. This upregulation was further corroborated at the protein level, with elevated zDHHC11 expression observed both in cultured cells and in brain tissue sections. Knockdown of Zdhhc11 suppressed cytokine expression/secretion and reduced TLR4/MyD88 levels, indicating that zDHHC11 acts upstream of this common pathway.
